source: Wong and Debroy (2009) A Survey of Software Fault Localization (UTD tech report UTDCS-45-09)
finding: Defines Tarantula suspiciousness as X/(X+Y): X is the share of failed tests that run the statement, Y the share of passed tests that run it. Notes it treats every failed test and every passed test as equal.
numbers: Formula only. Survey cites the Jones and Harrold Siemens study: Tarantula examines less code before the first faulty statement than set union, set intersection, nearest neighbour and cause transitions.
limits: Secondary report of the founding result; the Siemens numbers themselves are not in this text. Siemens faults are seeded, small C programs.
agent_relevance: Spectrum ranking is a cheap, code-computed signal. It can feed the agent a ranked list of suspect lines from test outcomes, no model opinion needed (G2).

source: Wong and Debroy (2009) survey, coincidental correctness
finding: Spectrum methods lose accuracy when a faulty line runs in a passing test by luck (coincidental correctness). Wang et al. found Tarantula worse when this is frequent and better when it is rare.
numbers: Ball et al. report coincidental correctness made their method miss the fault in 3 of 15 cases.
limits: Small early studies; the survey calls for more research.
agent_relevance: A passing test that touches a line does not clear it. The agent should not treat passing as proof the line is fine.

source: Wong and Debroy (2009) survey, section 4.4 missing-code faults
finding: Spectrum and slice methods point at executed code, so they cannot point at code that is absent. Faults from missing code need other signals.
numbers: No numbers.
quote: One claim that can be made against the fault localization methods is that they are incapable of locating a fault that is the result of missing code.
limits: Conceptual boundary, widely repeated.
agent_relevance: When the bug is an omission, code-located suspects will mislead. The agent needs a way to say nothing here, something is missing.

source: Wong et al. principle as described in the 2009 survey (diminishing returns of extra tests)
finding: Principle: the first failed test covering a line should count more than the second, and the second more than the third. Same for passed tests. Basis of the Wong family of formulas that the survey says are generally more effective than Tarantula.
numbers: No figures given in the survey for this comparison.
limits: Claim is as reported by the survey; the original paper was not opened.
agent_relevance: More failing runs help less and less. Two or three good failing traces are enough; more adds cost.

source: Weimer, Nguyen, Le Goues, Forrest (2009) Automatically Finding Patches Using Genetic Programming (ICSE)
finding: GenProg uses fault localisation as a search prior. Statements run only by the failing test get weight 1.0. Statements also run by passing tests get weight WPath=0.01. Mutation and crossover act mostly on failing-path statements. Fitness = 1 x passed positive tests + 10 x passed negative tests.
numbers: Ten C programs, 63,000 lines, repaired in under 200 s on average. Overall success rate 59%. Average 36.9 fitness evaluations. Final patch averaged about 4 lines after minimisation. Parameters WPath=0.01, Wmut=0.06, WPosT=1, WNegT=10.
quote: Taking WPath = 0 prevents us from considering any statement visited on a positive testcase
limits: Programs chosen by the authors. Later work (Qi 2015) found many GenProg patches were not correct.
agent_relevance: Founding design for locate, then edit only there. Narrowing the edit region by code-computed evidence is the same idea as G2.

source: Weimer et al. (2009) GenProg, what predicts success
finding: Repair success does not depend on the type of fault. It falls as the weighted path length grows, meaning the count of statements on the failing path but not on passing paths.
numbers: Infinite loops: 54% success. Buffer overruns: 61%. All faults: 59%.
quote: the success rate is inversely related to the weighted path length
limits: Ten programs only; no inferential test.
agent_relevance: How tightly the failure is localised, not the bug class, predicts repair success. Shrink the suspect set before asking for a fix.

source: Weimer et al. (2009) GenProg, minimisation step
finding: Raw evolved patches contain spurious edits. They are cut down with tree differencing and delta debugging until the patch is minimal and still passes the tests.
numbers: Example minimal patch 11 lines of diff (gcd case); average final patch 4 lines.
limits: Minimal is not the same as correct.
agent_relevance: Keep the final patch small and drop every edit not needed to remove the failing output.

source: Qi, Long, Achour, Rinard (2015) Is the cure worse than the disease? Overfitting in automated program repair (FSE)
finding: Re-check of GenProg, RSRepair and AE patches by hand found most plausible patches (pass the tests) are not correct; many just delete functionality. From memory of the paper, not opened (closed access).
numbers: Recalled figure, unverified here: GenProg correct on only 2 of the 105 bugs of its original benchmark. Semantic Scholar lists 432 citations.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Test-passing is weak evidence of a correct fix. Require the failing output gone and check nothing was deleted to get there.

source: Pearson et al. (2017) Evaluating and Improving Fault Localization (ICSE)
finding: Replicated spectrum and mutation fault localisation on real faults (Defects4J) rather than seeded ones. Results on artificial faults did not carry over to real faults. From memory; paper not opened (download URLs returned 404).
numbers: No figures verified.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Beware benchmark results from seeded bugs. Real bugs are harder to rank by spectrum alone.

source: Parnin and Orso (2011) Are automated debugging techniques actually helping programmers? (ISSTA)
finding: User study of whether ranked suspicious-statement lists help programmers. Recalled: no clear benefit on harder tasks, programmers did not follow the list in order, and the idea that seeing one line is enough is a hidden assumption. Not opened (closed access, HTTP 403).
numbers: Semantic Scholar lists 664 citations. No study numbers verified.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: A ranking is only useful if the consumer can use it. For a model the ranking is cheap to consume, but a line alone without context may still not be enough.

source: Kang, An, Yoo (2024) A Quantitative and Qualitative Evaluation of LLM-Based Explainable Fault Localization (AutoFL)
finding: AutoFL gives the LLM function-call tools to read the repository. It outputs a fault location plus an explanation. It beats spectrum (Ochiai) and mutation-based FL on method-level acc@1.
numbers: 798 real bugs (Defects4J v1.0 353 bugs, BugsInPy). GPT-3.5 beats Ochiai by 19.7% acc@1 on Defects4J and 166.7% on BugsInPy; GPT-4 by 233.3% on BugsInPy. Beats SmartFL on the 222-bug subset.
limits: Closure bugs excluded for the SmartFL comparison. Possible training-data leakage for old benchmarks. Acc@3 and acc@5 of GPT-3.5 lag SBFL.
agent_relevance: Models locate better when they can call tools to read code than when handed a file. Fits code-supplied evidence.

source: Kang et al. (2024) AutoFL, repeated runs and confidence
finding: Running AutoFL several times and merging gives a large gain. A single GPT-4 run beats five merged GPT-3.5 runs. The model stated confidence correlates with correctness.
numbers: Spearman between confidence and Precision@1: 0.57 (Defects4J) and 0.52 (BugsInPy); with reciprocal rank 0.67 and 0.50; all p<0.0001. Time: 16.4 s per run (GPT-3.5, Defects4J), 87.24 s for 5 runs plus prep, versus 112 s for SBFL; GPT-4 total 310 s.
limits: Correlation is moderate, not calibration. Confidence is the model own number.
agent_relevance: Sample the localiser several times and merge ranks. Use agreement across runs rather than one run confidence.

source: Kang et al. (2024) AutoFL, tool-use ablation
finding: Test-GPT3.5, which predicts the fault location with no function interaction, was consistently worse than AutoFL. GPT-3.5 has difficulty digging deep into a repository.
numbers: Shown in figure form; no single number extracted.
limits: Authors reading of traces.
agent_relevance: Give the agent a way to look things up, and expect weaker models to stop digging early.

source: Wu, Li, Zhang, Papadakis, Harman, Liu (2023) Large Language Models in Fault Localisation
finding: ChatGPT-3.5 and 4 prompted on Defects4J. Adding the failed-test error log helps. At function level GPT-4 with log beats all prior methods. At class level it collapses.
numbers: Mean Top-1: ChatGPT-4 with log 23.13 versus SmartFL 15.75 (+46.9%); ChatGPT-3.5 origin 13.60, with log 14.67; ChatGPT-4 origin 15.93. Class-level context: GPT-4 49.9% lower than SmartFL on Top-1.
quote: Additional error logs can further improve ChatGPT models' localisation accuracy and consistency
limits: Models from 2023. Sensitive to context length. Averages over repeated runs; counts small.
agent_relevance: Showing the real failing output raised accuracy in every setting tested. Direct support for G2. Long context hurts localisation.

source: Wu et al. (2023) repeated-run consistency
finding: Five repeated runs show run-to-run variation. GPT-4 with log is the most consistent; GPT-3.5 origin fluctuates most.
numbers: Table 4 Top-1 counts: ChatGPT-3.5 origin roughly 77 to 89 faults per run; ChatGPT-4 with log roughly 135 to 145 per run.
limits: Table text partly garbled in extraction; ranges approximate.
agent_relevance: Model localisation is noisy per run. Use several samples plus a code check.

source: Yang, Le Goues, Martins, Hellendoorn (2024) Large Language Models for Test-Free Fault Localization (LLMAO, ICSE)
finding: Fine-tunes small bidirectional adapter layers on frozen CodeGen models to score each code line as buggy, with no test coverage. Performance rises with model size.
numbers: 395 Defects4J v1.2 bugs, Top-1/3/5: Ochiai 19/65/99 (4.8/16.5/25.1%); DeepFL 57/95/135; TRANSFER-FL 86/135/160; LLMAO 350M 82/106/126; 6B 85/115/160; 16B 88/149/183 (22.3/37.7/46.3%). New projects: 72/93/123. Ablation: 6 layers from scratch 5/24/30; predict directly from 16B 10/60/85.
limits: Needs fine-tuning data. Top-1 only slightly above TRANSFER-FL. BugsInPy Top-1 10.3%, Devign 28.1%.
agent_relevance: A line-level localiser can work without tests, but test-free is much weaker than test-informed. Keep the failing output when it exists.

source: Qin et al. (2025) AgentFL: Scaling LLM-based Fault Localization to Project-Level Context
finding: Multi-agent ChatGPT system models fault localisation as comprehension, navigation, confirmation, with test-behaviour tracking and document-guided search.
numbers: 157 of 395 Defects4J v1.2.0 bugs at Top-1; 28 more than LLMAO+Ochiai and 36 more than ChatGPT+Ochiai.
limits: Authors benchmark; Closure did not improve. Cost not extracted.
agent_relevance: Staging the work as understand, search, then confirm with test evidence beat one-shot prompting for repository-scale localisation.

source: Xia, Wei, Zhang (2023) Practical Program Repair in the Era of Large Pre-trained Language Models
finding: Broad study of nine pre-trained LMs (125M to 20B) for repair on five datasets in three languages. Code after the buggy line (infilling) helps. Bigger models fix more. Codex beats all prior APR tools without fine-tuning.
numbers: Defects4J 1.2: INCODER 6.7B with 2000 samples plus templates fixed 78 bugs, 32 more than the best prior technique. Of 354 individual fixes, 234 (66%) differed from the developer patch (77% excluding single-line bugs).
limits: Perfect fault localisation assumed (location given). Leakage cannot be ruled out.
agent_relevance: Repair results in the literature assume the location is given. Locating is the harder, separately measured step.

source: Xia and Zhang (2024) Keep the Conversation Going: Fixing 162 out of 337 bugs for $0.42 each using ChatGPT (ChatRepair)
finding: Conversational repair: first feed the failing test output, then after each failed patch feed the new failing output and the previous failed or plausible patches.
numbers: 114 correct fixes on Defects4J 1.2 and 48 on 2.0, 15 and 17 more than the best prior tool. 162 of 337 bugs at about $0.42 each. Under 500 patches per bug versus up to 10,000 for earlier learning tools.
limits: Location given in the settings used. Possible leakage. ChatGPT worse than Codex on Defects4J 1.2 infilling per authors.
agent_relevance: Strong support for G2 and the revise step: revise from the actual failing output and keep a short history of failed attempts.

source: Bouzenia, Devanbu, Pradel (2024) RepairAgent: An Autonomous LLM-Based Agent for Program Repair
finding: Agent with a finite state machine and tools (read lines, search code, run tests, run fault localisation, write fix). Repairs 164 of 835 Defects4J bugs, including 39 not fixed by earlier techniques. About 270,000 tokens, 14 cents, per bug.
numbers: Average 35 tool calls per bug. Write-fix calls: 6 on fixed bugs, 17 on unfixed; 44% of write-fix calls on fixed bugs gave plausible patches versus 7% on unfixed.
limits: Default setting uses perfect fault localisation. Fails some single-line bugs that ChatRepair fixes.
agent_relevance: Failed bugs show many repeated write attempts. A cap on revision rounds fits.

source: RepairAgent, effect of realistic fault localisation
finding: Swapping perfect localisation for a real spectrum tool (GZoltar) lowers the repair rate and raises cost.
numbers: 25% drop in fixing capability and 81% increase in cost; text reports 16 bugs for 29 dollars in that run (subset size not stated in the lines read).
limits: Subset size unclear; one run.
agent_relevance: Published repair rates mostly assume perfect localisation. Real accuracy depends on how well the agent localises.

source: RepairAgent, memory ablation
finding: If the agent sees new information for one cycle only, fixing falls sharply: it repeats commands and uses wrong file or function names. Long-term memory of gathered facts helps.
numbers: No number extracted (figure only).
limits: Single benchmark.
agent_relevance: Keep a running record of facts found and tried; repeating the same lookup is a failure mode.

source: Zhang, Ruan, Fan, Roychoudhury (2024) AutoCodeRover: Autonomous Program Improvement (ISSTA)
finding: Code search over program structure (classes and methods) plus optional spectrum fault localisation. Spectrum hints sharpen the context given to the patch agent.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite (300 issues): 19.00% (57) at about $0.43 each; with SBFL 66 tasks resolved (about 22%). ACR with SBFL uniquely resolves 7 tasks not resolved in other runs.
limits: SBFL needs a runnable test suite; a full suite was built for this experiment. Runs are non-deterministic.
agent_relevance: Code-computed fault localisation raised repair success from 57 to 66 of 300. Direct support that code locates (G2).

source: Xia, Deng, Dunn, Zhang (2024) Agentless: Demystifying LLM-based Software Engineering Agents
finding: Three fixed steps, no agent loop: hierarchical localisation (file, then class or function, then edit lines), repair by sampled diffs, test-based selection. Localisation combines LLM prompting with embedding retrieval.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite: 32.00% (96 of 300) at $0.70 average, highest among open-source tools then. File localisation correct: prompting 78.7%, embedding 67.7%, combined 81.7%. Repair: greedy 88 (29.33%), 4x10 samples 96 (32.00%).
limits: Authors found problems in SWE-bench Lite (exact-patch leaks, vague issues) and built Lite-S. Leaderboards change fast.
agent_relevance: A fixed locate-then-repair pipeline matches complex agents. Narrowing file to function to lines fits a staged schema.

source: Agentless localisation ablation
finding: Skipping the class/function step and going directly from file to edit lines hurts. Passing whole files instead of a skeleton costs more. Model-written reproduction tests pick the final patch.
numbers: Context shrinks from over 3,000 to under 800 lines after class/function localisation.
limits: Exact ablation percentages not extracted line by line.
agent_relevance: Staged narrowing saves context and improves accuracy. A reproduction test makes the failure code-checkable.

source: Jimenez et al. (2024) SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues? (ICLR)
finding: 2,294 real issues from 12 Python repositories. With BM25 file retrieval the best model, Claude 2, resolves only 1.96%. Retrieval recall of the right files is poor.
numbers: BM25 recall of oracle files: 29.58, 44.41, 51.06 at growing context sizes. In about 40% of instances BM25 retrieves a superset of the oracle files.
limits: 2023 baseline; later systems resolve far more.
agent_relevance: Locating the right file is a bottleneck; later gains came from better localisation as much as better fixing.

source: Yang et al. (2024) SWE-agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces Enable Automated Software Engineering
finding: A custom interface with search, file view and guarded edit commands lets GPT-4 Turbo resolve issues far above non-interactive models. Interface design alone changes success.
numbers: 12.47% of 2,294 SWE-bench tasks; 87.7% pass@1 on HumanEvalFix.
limits: ACI ablation figures only partly read.
agent_relevance: Concise feedback per action and guardrails against bad edits matter. Code should control what the model sees.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation? (ICLR)
finding: Models give poor feedback on their own failing code. Under equal sample budget self-repair gives modest gains and sometimes none versus plain sampling.
numbers: GPT-4 on APPS: 10 initial samples plus 1 repair each gives 1.05x the pass@20 baseline; 2 samples plus 10 repairs each gives 0.97x pass@22.
limits: Self-contained Python tasks (HumanEval, APPS), not repository bugs.
agent_relevance: Self-diagnosis by the same model is the weak link. Supports G2: revisions need evidence from output, not self-opinion.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) self-repair, feedback quality
finding: Replacing the model own explanation with a stronger model or a human raises repair. Human feedback raises GPT-4 repair success from 33.3% to 52.6%.
numbers: GPT-4 vs human feedback: introductory 42.64% vs 62.21%; interview 19.33% vs 45.67%; competition 3.67% vs 14.67%; overall 33.30% vs 52.60%.
limits: Small human study; participant count not extracted here.
agent_relevance: Quality of the diagnosis (the locate step) is the lever. Give the repair step concrete localised evidence.
